claim: Chemical probes are powerful research reagents that are potent, selective and broadly characterized small molecule modulators of protein function.
source: Potent, selective and broadly characterized small molecule modulators of protein function (chemical probes) are powerful research reagents.
evidence: This is a definitional statement in the abstract that establishes what chemical probes are and their utility.

claim: The pharmaceutical industry has generated many high-quality chemical probes.
source: The pharmaceutical industry has generated many high-quality chemical probes and several of these have been made available to academia.
evidence: This is a general statement about the pharmaceutical industry's contribution to chemical probe development.

claim: Probe-associated data and control compounds are generally not accessible from pharmaceutical companies.
source: However, probe-associated data and control compounds, such as inactive structurally related molecules and their associated data, are generally not accessible.
evidence: This statement describes the current state of accessibility of probe-related materials.

claim: Seven pharmaceutical companies (AbbVie, Bayer, Boehringer Ingelheim, Janssen, MSD, Pfizer, and Takeda) have entered into a pre-competitive collaboration to make available chemical probes.
source: Several pharmaceutical companies (AbbVie, Bayer, Boehringer Ingelheim, Janssen, MSD, Pfizer, and Takeda) have therefore entered into a pre-competitive collaboration to make available a large number of innovative high-quality probes, including all probe-associated data, control compounds and recommendations on use (https://openscienceprobes.sgc-frankfurt.de/).
evidence: This describes the specific collaboration established for this project.

claim: Genetic approaches using siRNA, shRNA, or CRISPR/Cas9 are used to suppress gene/protein expression.
source: Genetic approaches are used to suppress the expression of the respective gene/protein, for example using gene editing methods such as siRNA or shRNA or by CRISPR/Cas9 (Mali et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement describes established genetic methods and cites a reference for support.

claim: Genetic approaches commonly remove or suppress the entire protein and cannot easily reveal the function of a specific druggable protein domain.
source: However, in drug discovery, these methods have some deficiencies: they commonly remove or suppress the entire protein and thus cannot easily reveal the function of a specific druggable protein domain – although domain-based CRISPR is becoming a more widely used method
evidence: This describes limitations of genetic approaches compared to chemical probes.

claim: Genetic approaches are not reversible.
source: they are not reversible
evidence: This is stated as one of the deficiencies of genetic methods in drug discovery.

claim: Genetic approaches' effects are not instantaneous.
source: their effects are not instantaneous
evidence: This is stated as one of the deficiencies of genetic methods in drug discovery.

claim: Genetic approaches not only disrupt the protein but also the protein interactome around the targeted protein.
source: they not only disrupt the protein, but also the protein interactome around the targeted protein
evidence: This describes a limitation of genetic approaches.

claim: Selective small molecule modulators can probe the particular function of a targeted domain.
source: Selective small molecule modulators ('chemical probes'), in contrast, can probe the particular function of a targeted domain and can, therefore, be used to study its role in biological processes and in human disease in a dose and time-dependent manner across a wide range of cell and animal models.
evidence: This describes the capabilities of chemical probes in contrast to genetic methods.

claim: Chemical probes can be used to study protein roles in biological processes and human disease in a dose and time-dependent manner.
source: Selective small molecule modulators ('chemical probes'), in contrast, can probe the particular function of a targeted domain and can, therefore, be used to study its role in biological processes and in human disease in a dose and time-dependent manner across a wide range of cell and animal models.
evidence: This describes the utility of chemical probes.

claim: Chemical probes can be modified to enhance the degradation of the protein(s) they bind to.
source: These probes can also be modified to enhance the degradation of the protein(s) they bind to (Mali et al., 2013; Toure and Crews, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Small molecules can be used in a broad panel of assay systems comprising primary cells, tissues and in vivo models.
source: Small molecules can be used in a broad panel of assay systems comprising primary cells, tissues and also in vivo models, and other systems not easily amenable even for state-of-the-art genetic target validation methods.
evidence: This describes the versatility of small molecules in various experimental systems.

claim: Having a panel of selective probes that can be used in combination will facilitate data deconvolution and target identification.
source: Despite the fact that non-selective compounds cast a wide net and can be used to uncover interesting polypharmacologies, having a panel of selective probes that can be used in combination will facilitate data deconvolution and target identification.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of selective probes in research.

claim: Chemical probes have the possibility of further development into drug candidates.
source: These properties, together with the possibility of further development of probes into drug candidates, make them among the most versatile tools to explore the relevance of a protein for therapeutic development.
evidence: This describes one of the advantages of chemical probes.

claim: Necessary characterization data is often missing for chemical compounds.
source: However, the necessary characterization data is often missing for chemical compounds, and inhibitors are announced as being 'selective' despite missing a comprehensive profile.
evidence: This describes a problem in the field of chemical probes.

claim: Tool compounds that are chemically unstable or not comprehensively characterized are limited in their utility.
source: Tool compounds, which are chemically unstable or not comprehensively characterized are therefore limited in their utility (Arrowsmith et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Poorly characterized chemical modulators generate misleading results and litter the literature with contradicting data on a target's function.
source: Moreover, poorly characterized chemical modulators generate misleading results and litter the literature with contradicting data on a target's function and its role in biology.
evidence: This describes the negative consequences of using poorly characterized compounds.

claim: Reactive and non-specific inhibitors are widely used in the academic research community, often resulting in incorrect functional annotation.
source: Unfortunately, reactive and non-specific inhibitors are widely used in the academic research community, often resulting in incorrect functional annotation (Baell and Walters, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The ideal chemical probes need to be selective, active in cells and chemically stable.
source: The ideal chemical probes need to be selective, active in cells and chemically stable.
evidence: This defines the key criteria for ideal chemical probes.

claim: The chemical biology community has suggested stringent quality criteria for chemical probes.
source: The recent discussion on best practice within the chemical biology community suggested a number of stringent quality criteria for chemical probes (Arrowsmith et al., 2015; Blagg and Workman, 2017; Edwards et al., 2009; Bunnage et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Structural Genomics Consortium applies specific criteria for chemical probes as shown in Figure 1.
source: Typical criteria as applied by the Structural Genomics Consortium (SGC) are shown in Figure 1, although these may vary slightly depending on the specific protein.
evidence: This refers to specific criteria shown in a figure.

claim: Characterization data associated with chemical tool compounds are often either incomplete or buried in patents or supplemental data files of publications.
source: However, characterization data associated with these compounds are often either incomplete or buried in patents or supplemental data files of publications.
evidence: This describes a problem with accessibility of compound characterization data.

claim: The Chemical Probes Portal was established in 2015 to provide a comprehensive overview of published and newly released tool compounds.
source: Help is provided for example by the Chemical Probes Portal (Baell and Walters, 2014; Blagg and Workman, 2017), which was established in 2015 to provide a comprehensive overview of published and newly released tool compounds that are annotated with a simple star-rating system.
evidence: This provides factual information about when the portal was established and its purpose.

claim: All compounds submitted to the Chemical Probes Portal are reviewed by at least three members of an independent expert scientific advisory board.
source: All compounds submitted to the portal are reviewed by at least three members of an independent expert scientific advisory board.
evidence: This describes the review process for the Chemical Probes Portal.

claim: Only probes that receive three or four stars from the Chemical Probes Portal are recommended to be used.
source: Only probes that receive three stars ('Best available probe for this target, or a high-quality probe that is a useful orthogonal tool') or four stars ('Recommended as a probe for this target') are recommended to be used.
evidence: This describes the rating system and recommendations of the portal.

claim: Of about 400 compounds submitted to the Chemical Probes Portal, 125 have achieved a rating of three stars or better.
source: Of all the compounds submitted to the probe portal so far (about 400), 125 have achieved a rating of three stars or better, thereby showing that there is an urgent need for more high-quality tool compounds to foster reproducible research.
evidence: This provides specific data about the portal's compound ratings.

claim: There is an urgent need for more high-quality tool compounds to foster reproducible research.
source: Of all the compounds submitted to the probe portal so far (about 400), 125 have achieved a rating of three stars or better, thereby showing that there is an urgent need for more high-quality tool compounds to foster reproducible research.
evidence: This is inferred from the low proportion of compounds meeting quality standards.

claim: Probe development is a multi-disciplinary effort involving experts from several areas including protein chemistry, biochemistry, cell biology, pharmacology and medicinal chemistry.
source: Like drug discovery, probe development is a multi-disciplinary effort involving experts from several areas including protein chemistry, biochemistry, cell biology, pharmacology and medicinal chemistry (Dahlin and Walters, 2014; Garbaccio and Parmee, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: A typical screening cascade for a kinase probe discovery project is shown in Figure 2.
source: A typical screening cascade for a kinase probe discovery project is shown in Figure 2.
evidence: This refers to a figure showing the screening process.

claim: The screening cascade consists of a primary assay, an assay with an orthogonal readout, selectivity assays, and a cell-based assay.
source: The screening cascade consists of a primary assay – usually a biochemical activity assay – plus an assay with an orthogonal readout, e.g., a biophysical assay, a number of selectivity assays for the target and a cell-based assay to demonstrate on-target activity in the cellular environment.
evidence: This describes the components of a typical screening cascade.

claim: Multiple rounds of the Design – Make – Test – Analyze circle are needed before a suitable probe candidate is identified.
source: For a typical project, multiple rounds of the Design – Make – Test – Analyze circle (Plowright et al., 2012) are needed before a suitable probe candidate is identified.
evidence: This describes the iterative process of probe development with citation support.

claim: Experience within the SGC shows that approximately 1–2 years and €2 million are needed to generate one chemical probe fulfilling stringent criteria.
source: Experience within the SGC shows that approximately 1–2 years and €2 million are needed to generate one chemical probe fulfilling these stringent criteria (Donner, 2014).
evidence: This provides specific data about the time and cost of probe development with citation support.

claim: A suitable control compound should have a chemical structure closely related to that of the probe but lacking activity on the target.
source: A way to reduce the risk of non-specific effects is the use of a suitable control compound having a chemical structure closely related to that of the probe but lacking activity on the target.
evidence: This describes the characteristics of an appropriate control compound.

claim: Having access to multiple probes from structurally different chemical series reduces the risk that unknown off-target activities give rise to incorrect conclusions about target functions.
source: Having access to multiple probes from structurally different chemical series further reduces the risk that unknown off-target activities give rise to incorrect conclusions about target functions.
evidence: This describes a strategy to improve research reliability.

claim: Many quality probe compounds are buried in the chemical vaults of the pharmaceutical industry.
source: Many quality probe compounds are buried in the chemical vaults of the pharmaceutical industry, depriving the scientific community of useful tools and limiting the impact of the original research.
evidence: This describes the current state of probe accessibility.

claim: In the nuclear hormone receptor field, any legal encumbrances to compound access reduced the subsequent use of the compound in the literature significantly.
source: Indeed, in the nuclear hormone receptor field, we showed that any legal encumbrances to compound access reduced the subsequent use of the compound in the literature significantly (Isserlin, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: The open access/open science approach is the fastest route to reach the end users and have a positive effect on research.
source: Thus, the open access/open science approach is the fastest route to reach the end users and thereby to have a positive effect on research.
evidence: This is inferred from the previous evidence about legal encumbrances.

claim: Seven pharmaceutical companies associated with the SGC have each agreed to donate 10 compounds, for a total of 70 high-quality small molecules.
source: To this end, seven pharmaceutical companies associated with the SGC have each agreed to donate 10 of these valuable compounds, stemming from their research pipelines, for a total of 70 high-quality small molecules, thus providing a major boost to the chemical biology toolbox.
evidence: This provides specific data about the number of compounds being donated.

claim: Not all donated probes have been profiled to the same depth that is required of a high-quality chemical probe.
source: As the primary focus of the pharmaceutical industry is not to generate chemical probes, but to develop new drugs, not all donated probes have been profiled to the same depth that is required of a high-quality chemical probe.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the donated probes.

claim: Specificity for a particular target is not a requirement for an effective drug.
source: Moreover, specificity for a particular target is not a requirement for an effective drug.
evidence: This is a statement about drug development principles.

claim: Once broadly characterized and accompanied by relevant control compounds, the initial set of 70 probes reflect a collective contribution of at least €140 million to the public domain.
source: Once broadly characterized and accompanied by relevant control compounds, the initial set of 70 probes reflect a collective contribution of at least €140 million to the public domain (Figure 3).
evidence: This provides a specific valuation of the probe contribution.

claim: The donated probes cover a broad array of targets from different protein families relevant for a number of disease indications.
source: These donated probes cover a broad array of targets from different protein families relevant for a number of disease indications (see Table 1).

source: An excellent example of a donated probe is the recently published p300/CBP histone acetyltransferase (HAT) inhibitor (A-485), which was shown to have efficacy in several cell models of malignancies (Lasko et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: The donated probe candidates and control compounds are subjected to a two-tier scientific review process.
source: In order to guarantee the quality of the compounds, the donated probe candidates and control compounds are subjected to a two-tier scientific review process: the first review takes place internally, including partners who have not been involved in the probe project, and the second review is performed by a panel of renowned scientists, who have agreed to act as independent reviewers.
evidence: This describes the quality control process for the donated probes.

claim: The first 30 proposals were presented to the internal review committee during a two-day meeting in June 2017 in Frankfurt am Main, Germany.
source: The first 30 proposals were presented to the internal review committee during a two-day meeting in June 2017 in Frankfurt am Main, Germany, where a process for their release to the public was also established.
evidence: This provides specific factual information about the review meeting.

claim: A maximum of two chemical probes for the same target will be accepted if they represent different chemotypes.
source: In the initial set, most targets are uniquely addressed by only one chemical compound, but a maximum of two chemical probes for the same target will be accepted if they represent different chemotypes as judged by the review panels.
evidence: This describes a policy for probe selection.

claim: All approved probes will be profiled in assay panels comprising of >500 assays.
source: All approved probes are measured against the same quality criteria (Figure 1) and will be profiled in assay panels comprising of >500 assays, including broad panels of pharmacologically active targets such as GPCRs, kinases, ion channels and proteases to identify off-target activities (Table 2).

claim: Disease-specific phenotypic panels will provide an initial characterization of the probes' biological effects.

claim: The thinking in pharmaceutical R&D has shifted over the last decade, with more challenges seen as precompetitive.
source: While in the past almost all aspects of pharmaceutical research and development (R&D) were seen as competitive, the thinking in the field has shifted remarkably over the last decade. More and more challenges in the R&D process are seen as precompetitive, resulting in public–private partnerships and multilateral, critical mass consortia jointly addressing overarching issues.
